newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher, inflation outlook tame.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher, inflation outlook tame.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended sharply up on Thursday, boosted by some friendly economic data and a substantial drop in commodity prices, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at the day's highs to quote up 26/32 at 101-12/32. Its yield slid to 6.64 percent, one of the lowest levels in seven months.

The buying spree was triggered by the release of fresh data suggesting the economy is continuing to slow with no sign of inflation. The rally gained extra momentum after commodity prices slumped late in the afternoon session.
"The thing that's really driving the market is this collapse in commodity prices today," said Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust.
"Oil has collapsed; copper is weak; the CRB is down sharply and I think this is giving some support to the market," Kasriel added.

The Commodity Research Bureau (CRB) Index was quoted down 3.8 points (1.58 percent) at 237.83 in late trading. December crude oil traded at the New York Mercantile Exchange was off $1.09 at $23.19 a barrel in the late afternoon session.
Analysts said the sharp drop in commodity prices may ease some lurking fears that inflation data for October could be influenced by a recent run-up in energy prices.

"Some people were getting a bit anxious about the upcoming producer and consumer price indices," said a trader at a U.S. bank. "But the drop in commodity prices today, if sustained, could wipe out those fears."
The PPI and CPI data for October will be released on November 13 and November 14, respectively.
In the morning session, the market took its cue from a sharp rise in weekly jobless claims data.
The indicator showed claims for jobless benefits rose to 342,000 in the week ended October 26 from a revised 319,000 in the previous week.
Although labor markets are still seen as tight, analysts said that a relief in the weekly claims figures encouraged some investing in fixed-income securities.
The market also welcomed the release of a market-friendly Chicago Purchasing Managers Index for October.
Although the overall business activity index rose slightly to 56.9 (53.3 in September), analysts said the market cheered after prices paid dropped to 50.7 against 59.3 earlier.
The market also took in some fresh data saying September personal income rose 0.6 percent, while spending was up 0.1 percent. The U.S. savings rate was at 5.7 percent.
"We saw another good increase in income ... but it looks like people are either buying stocks with their extra income or they're paying down some of their debt," Kasriel said.

The market also absorbed some $17.0 billion in 48-day cash management bills. The Treasury managed to place the securities at 5.17 percent. After Thursday's rally, the market's eyes are now focused on the release of the key employment report for October on Friday.
In a Reuters poll, analysts expect non-farm payrolls to rise by 212,000 in October against a 40,000 drop in the previous month.

Analysts said the number could create some volatilty. But they added that given Treasuries' current bullish tone it would take a huge distortion in the data to take the wind out of the market's sails.
Cary Leahey, senior financial markets economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, said payrolls would have to print 400,000 to really "rock Treasuries."
New jobs totalling 300,000, he said, "won't do it."
To the upside for prices, Leahey said, "the sky is the limit" if payrolls print only about 125,000.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up one basis point at 5.02 percent. The six-month bill rate fell one point to 5.07 percent. The year bill rate was down three points at 5.14 percent.

The two-year note closed up 3/32 at 100-7/32, yielding 5.76 percent. The five-year note traded up 9/32 at 100-24/32 to yield 6.07 percent. The ten-year note closed up 16/32 at 101-5/32, yielding 6.34 percent.
